title: How do we turn a fraction into a decimal?
description: Three fractions with ten, hundred and thousand parts are split into tenths, hundredths and thousandths, then read as decimals. Keeko doubts that eight hundred and forty seven over ten thousand is zero point eight four seven.
teaching_notes: One idea: split the top into hundreds, tens and ones, and let each piece find its own place after the point. Watch for students who forget the extra zero when the bottom is ten thousand.

source: Write 847/10000, 173/100 and 23/1000 as a sum of tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and as decimals
video_script.why: The child can read tenths and hundredths and now sees how a fraction with a bigger power of ten as its bottom becomes a decimal.
video_script.substitution: the three fractions of the book's table, with the first row of the table as the model
video_script.anchor: The table of fractions from the book: each fraction is split into tenths, hundredths and thousandths and then written as a decimal
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip writes eight hundred and forty seven over ten thousand as zero point eight four seven. That is over one thousand, so a zero is missing after the point.
video_script.payoff_line: Each fraction is now a sum and a decimal.

final_answer.spoken: zero point zero eight four seven, one point seven three and zero point zero two three

maths_rules: the slip: 0.847 = 847/1000, which is ten times 847/10000
video_script.design: One idea: split the top by place value and let each piece land in its own place. Assumes tenths and hundredths. Wrong idea: three places for a fraction over ten thousand. The table stays all video; each row is added under the first row; decimals appear only on the answer beat.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Look at the first row of the table, two hundred and fifty four over one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Split the top into two hundred, fifty and four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each piece over one thousand cuts down to a tenth, a hundredth or a thousandth. Each of these is a decimal on its own.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, three fractions.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first is eight hundred and forty seven over ten thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The second is one hundred and seventy three over one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The third is twenty three over one thousand.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, split the top of the first fraction by place value, into eight hundred, forty and seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Cut each piece down. We get eight hundredths, four thousandths and seven ten thousandths.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>As decimals these are zero point zero eight and zero point zero zero four. The last piece is zero point zero zero zero seven.

marks.m2: the pieces become one, seven tenths and three hundredths
marks.m3: the pieces are written as decimals

beats.colours: each piece in its own colour
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, split the top of the second fraction into one hundred, seventy and three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred over one hundred is one whole. Seventy over one hundred is seven tenths, and three over one hundred stays.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>As decimals these are one, zero point seven and zero point zero three.

marks.m2: the pieces become two hundredths and three thousandths
marks.m3: the pieces are written as decimals

beats.colours: each piece in its own colour
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, split the top of the third fraction into twenty and three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twenty over one thousand is two hundredths. Three over one thousand is three thousandths.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>As decimals these are zero point zero two and zero point zero zero three.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Each fraction is now a sum and a decimal.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first is zero point zero eight four seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The second is one point seven three, and the third is zero point zero two three.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the first fraction is zero point eight four seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But that has three places after the point, so it means eight hundred and forty seven thousandths.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Our fraction is over ten thousand, so it needs four places. A zero goes in after the point.
